awd_titl_txt: SBIR Phase I: Development of rod-shaped drug delivery nanoparticles for in-space manufacturing
awd_abstract_narration:
The broader impact of this Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) Phase I project is its potential to transform the solid tumor cancer treatment market, projected to reach $424.6 billion by 2027. The project aims to advance the regulatory pathway for space-made medicines by using Janus base nanoparticles (JBNps) as a test case to demonstrate comparability with Earth-made versions. This step is crucial for the commercialization of space-made therapeutics, addressing challenges in drug delivery for solid tumors and advancing oncology biotherapeutics. Additionally, the project will boost U.S. dominance in the space economy, drive innovation and economic growth in biotech, and enhance the nation’s global competitiveness. It could lead to advanced, safer therapies for various diseases and contribute to fostering a diverse American STEM (Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics) workforce. Beyond its technological benefits, this project emphasizes diversity, education, and community outreach, promising broader societal and environmental benefits. Ultimately, it holds potential for positive impacts on the LEO (Low Earth Orbit) commercial space economy and global healthcare.

This Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) Phase I project aims to tackle the urgent need for advanced drug delivery systems capable of effectively targeting solid tumors. Current lipid nanoparticles (LNPs), while widely used, face challenges in penetrating the dense extracellular matrix (ECM) of tumors. Eascra’s project focuses on creating a regulatory pathway to commercialize space-made Janus base nanoparticles (JBNps). These nanoparticles, with their nano-rod morphology and DNA-mimicking chemistry, offer improved tumor penetration, effective treatment, and minimal toxicity. Additionally, JBNps maintain drug stability and bioactivity at room temperature, overcoming the cold storage challenges faced by LNPs. Phase I will advance the regulatory approval pathway, laying the groundwork for Phase II, where in-space manufacturing of JBNps will be optimized. This technology has the potential to revolutionize cancer treatment by providing a versatile, more effective drug delivery platform. The success of this project holds significant implications for future space-made medicines, benefiting both terrestrial and space-based healthcare.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
Chronic kidney disease affects about 15% of US adults. mRNA and RNA drugs could in principle treat it, but there is currently no reliable way to deliver them to the kidney. Most new genetic medicines such as small RNA or mRNA drugs, only work if they can be carried inside the cells that need them. The carriers used today, lipid nanoparticles (LNPs), are very good at reaching the liver and poor at reaching almost anywhere else. This limitation stems from the size of LNPs, which are spherical particles measuring roughly 80 to 100 nanometers. In contrast, biological barriers feature far smaller openings: the dense protein mesh surrounding cells in solid tumors and cartilage leaves gaps of just 10 to 20 nanometers, and the kidney's glomerular filtration barrier similarly presents a pore size of only 20 nanometers. An LNP sphere cannot fit through. Therefore, many have started to raise the dosages to compensate for concentrations on the drug in the liver causing unwanted side effects.

This project developed a different drug delivery carrier. Our project focused on improving how medicines are delivered into dense extracellular matrix (ECM), such as cartilage, solid tumors, and kidney, which remains difficult to treat effectively. The Janus Base Nanoparticle (JBNp) is built from engineered molecules that self-assemble into Janus base nanotubes (JBNts), which are then combined with cargo to form rod-shaped particles. A rod can pass through a gap that blocks a sphere. The material contains no lipids, avoiding the anti-carrier immune responses limiting how often lipid carriers can be re-dosed.

Phase I had two goals: to fabricate these novel delivery particles reliably to consistent specifications and to demonstrate their functional delivery performance. To achieve this, the team developed standardized methods to synthesize and characterize JBNp formulations that meet rigorous regulatory criteria. Using a streamlined one-pot reaction strategy, the fabrication process was optimized for reliable scalability and reproducible assembly under controlled conditions.

The project established that the rod particle shape of JBNps can be manufactured consistently in a controlled setting, by varying energy and duration of mixing step.  A library of formulations was prepared across a range of surface chemistries and cargo ratios and measured for size and uniformity. All measurements used internationally recognized standard methods, so the results can be compared against other laboratories and used to support future regulatory filings. The team also moved production from hand mixing onto a small continuous-flow chip, which is a step toward automated manufacture that can be documented under a quality system.

The JBNts were non-toxic to healthy cells, leaving more than 90% alive, which was better than all four conventional carriers tested, at every dose. They delivered genetic cargo into more than 80% of target cells, and in 3D in vitro models tumor tissue in which they traveled through the full thickness of the tissue while LNPs stayed at the surface. Cells receiving cargo from these particles produced roughly twice as much of the intended protein as cells given the same cargo by LNPs. In cartilage, a tissue that is dense, negatively charged, with no blood supply of its own, the rods traveled roughly eight times further into the tissue than LNPs, and reached cartilage after injection into the bloodstream rather than directly into the joint. In preliminary animal models, intravenously administered JBNp accumulated predominantly in the kidney instead of the liver, reversing the accumulation patterns seen with conventional delivery carriers, and successfully delivered functional cargo upon arrival. The kidney represents another anatomical site with tight glomerular filtration pores that routinely impede standard carriers. Messenger RNA was translated into protein inside kidney tubule cells, and a gene-editing cargo produced editing in the same cells. These data are early and the number of formulations tested was small, but they identify the kidney as a tissue this platform can reach. The project established that the JBNps kept their structure and most of their delivery ability for eight weeks at room temperature, suggesting JBNp may not require the refrigerated supply chains that current genetic medicines depend on. 

Delivery to the kidney is a recognized unmet need, and the evidence required to move any delivery technology toward development is well established: how a carrier distributes in the body, how it behaves over time, and how it is tolerated on repeat dosing across species. Generating that package for renal delivery is the company’s current priority.

While continuous-flow manufacturing requires further refinement to match manual consistency, evaluating particle distribution, dosing, and safety remains essential. Establishing these parameters is critical for securing pharmaceutical partnerships and validating this delivery platform. These focus areas define the next phase priorities. By enabling genetic medicine delivery to previously inaccessible tissues, this technology could become a leading nanotherapeutic for currently untreatable conditions, including major joint and kidney diseases.
